Disturbances within the monsoon trough are promoting an active
weather regime just north and west of the Marianas this afternoon,
while the southernmost islands experience a relative lull. Moderate 
to strong westerlies are expected to continue across the area over 
the next few days, increasing Sunday through Monday as the remnants 
of 13W swing east-southeastward, dipping over or near the far 
northern CNMI leading to a resurgence in monsoon winds across the 
area. Model guidance shows the southern edge of the developing 
monsoon surge shifting over Tinian and Saipan, maintaining breezy 
conditions and scattered showers there for much of the coming week.
A major factor in the short-term forecast concerns the remnants of 
13W, which are currently rated as "low" for development by the Joint 
Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC), meaning 13W is being monitored but is 
not expected to develop into a significant tropical cyclone in the 
next day or so. Some deterministic models do show 13W quickly 
developing north of the Marianas before it races off to the east- 
northeast, following behind Invest 98W. The magnitude and rate of 
13W's development, as well as how far south its track takes it, will 
be the main influencing factors in the strength of the monsoon surge 
across the CNMI over the next few days.

Marine/Surf...
Moderate to strong westerlies prevail across the Marianas as 
another resurgence in the monsoon builds over the northern CNMI, 
likely to maintain moderate to strong winds through the middle of 
next week, with the strongest winds expected over Tinian and 
Saipan waters. Combined seas of 8 to 11 feet are expected over the
next few days, remaining hazardous to small craft through at 
least early Tuesday morning. Seas look to fall below hazardous 
levels for Guam and Rota by midweek, but are expected to remain 
hazardous for Tinian and Saipan into the latter half of the week 
as the southern edge of the monsoon surge persists over the area. 
So, the Small Craft Advisory was extended for Guam and Rota waters
through early Tuesday morning, and Tinian and Saipan waters 
through Thursday afternoon.

Meanwhile, hazardous surf and a high risk of rip currents are 
expected to continue along west and north facing reefs through 
the middle of next week, and the High Surf Advisory and High Rip
Current Risk have been extended through Thursday afternoon. A 
moderate risk of lightning is expected Sunday through early next
week, mainly for Tinian and Saipan.

Tropical Systems...
Invest 98W continues to gradually organize. It's now located roughly
120 miles east of the Maug Islands near 19N 147.5E. The ECENS and 
GEFS are much more aligned with one another today regarding both the 
development and movement of 98W, and the remnants of 13W (currently 
near 20N 139E). It now looks like sufficient wave separation will 
exist between the remnants and 98W, as both models also try to 
develop a LLCC (Low-Level Circulation Center) with it. As 98W slowly
intensifies and lifts northeast to the north of Wake Island, the 
remnants and its developing circulation gradually develop and head on
a similar track, with all of this occurring over the next 48 to 72 
hours. Beyond that...stay tuned!

Then, looking farther south and east in the "very long range of
forecasting", a lead wave (surface circulation) currently northeast
of Majuro near 10N177E, looks to drift west for the next 24 hours,
then southwest and become quasi-stationary, while remaining at the 
tail end of a monsoon trough's eastern edge (the monsoon trough is in
the process of retreating to the west, slowly). As this occurs, a 
disturbance east of the Date Line near 8N177W on the 925mb analysis 
looks to also continue west, eventually developing a LLCC.

With the lead wave, a moisture surge (advection) is occurring, with
significantly higher PWATs (Precipitable water values increase from 
~1.5 inches ahead of it, to above 2.5 inches along and east of it.
So, essentially the lead wave is "preconditioning the environment, 
making it more favorable for later cyclogenesis (the formation of a 
LLCC). Then, as the circulation currently east of the Date Line 
catches of to the lead wave that makes a "pit stop" north of 
Kosrae/east of Pohnpei/west of Majuro and the RMI. Some guidance 
suggests a better-organized LLCC will develop 6 to 8 days from now 
(probably more so 7-9 days, as the models tend to have a +24 hour 
bias at this forecast range).

Normally, we wouldn't mention something this far out, but, having
already had a busy "dry" (quiet) season, and since we're just now
starting to enter the busier "wet" season, we just wanted folks to
know that we're watching it. As we typically state at anything beyond
5 days, it's way, way too early to say what will happen (will the
system develop, how strong will it be, where will it go, and when).
Just know we're keeping an eye on it, and continue to stay informed.
